title: Newborn Screening: Early Identification and Treatment
summary: The RUSP, dried blood spot testing, expanded panels, and the future of NBS with genomic sequencing.

content_blocks.text: Newborn screening (NBS) is one of public health's greatest success stories — a systematic population-based program that identifies babies with treatable metabolic, endocrine, hemoglobin, and other disorders before symptoms appear, enabling pre-symptomatic treatment that prevents death and disability. All 50 US states mandate NBS; the federal Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (RUSP) establishes minimum standards.

content_blocks.label: US newborns screened annually
content_blocks.context: NBS identifies approximately 12,500 affected infants per year across the ~35 RUSP core conditions; treatment prevents >1,000 infant deaths annually

rows: PAH enzyme deficiency → phenylalanine accumulation → brain damage
Phenylalanine-restricted diet; sapropterin (BH4) for responsive variants
Thyroid hormone deficiency → intellectual disability, growth failure
Levothyroxine — normal development if started within 2 weeks
Penicillin prophylaxis, hydroxyurea, transcranial doppler screening
T-cell lymphopenia → fatal infections without BMT
Hematopoietic stem cell transplant before infection exposure
SMN1 deletion → motor neuron loss → respiratory failure
Gene therapy (onasemnogene) before symptom onset achieves near-normal outcomes

content_blocks.text: Traditional NBS uses biochemical assays (MS/MS, enzyme assays, HPLC) that detect metabolic abnormalities — not genomic variants directly. Genomic NBS pilots (BabySeq, NC NEXUS, BeginNGS) are testing whether WGS or WES at birth can identify actionable conditions beyond the current RUSP panel, including rare conditions missed by biochemical screening and pharmacogenomic variants relevant to future drug exposures.

content_blocks.body: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) added to the RUSP in 2018, and 50 states now screen for it. Onasemnogene abeparvovec (Zolgensma) — a $2.1M single-dose gene therapy — replaces the non-functional SMN1 gene. When given before symptom onset (days to weeks of life), >90% of treated infants achieve normal motor milestones. After symptom onset, outcomes are dramatically worse. NBS makes the difference between a normal life and severe disability.
content_blocks.title: SMA Gene Therapy: Timing Is Everything
